prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from the experimental Higgs discovery (B046) to optical lattice clocks (B053) with Katori and Ye. In round 1 I said that if no individuals could be fairly singled out for the Higgs experiments, the clocks would be the more defensible choice, and the exchange has shown that this is the situation we are in. Pearce, Johansson and I each proposed a different trio from Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and nobody has produced an argument that would settle which founder is left out. A prize for two collaborations of thousands that is visibly arbitrary on names would not serve the discovery it wants to honour, and I put the discovery first. The clock case, by contrast, is what I look for: a magic-wavelength lattice that removes the first-order shifts, performance near 1e-18 reproduced independently at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL, and measurements in which nature is actually queried, such as the gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres and bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings. Those fundamental results are so far null, but a tight null bound on a theoretically motivated effect is a clue from nature, and it is the sort of result that has sent theorists back to their approximations before. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist and fits the statutes without a compromise on names.
statement.case_against: My reservation from round 1 is reduced but not removed. This is the third prize in a precision time-and-frequency line (combs in 2005 with Ye, ion control in 2012), and the largest payoff, the redefinition of the second and clock-based geodesy, is still ahead. I would have preferred the Higgs experiments if the credit could be fairly settled, because that discovery is more central to our understanding of nature and has waited fourteen years since the 2013 theory prize. Moving to B053 also gives up the discovery that I judge more fundamental in favour of the one that I judge more defensible, and I want that trade-off to be on the record. Finally, the Sr-lattice priority history between Tokyo and JILA, SYRTE, PTB and NIST is unverified, and a citation that cannot survive that check would be a serious embarrassment. Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy record look right, but that should be confirmed by expert reports and not assumed.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clocks first and answered my round-1 question by arguing that the comparisons (millimetre-scale redshift, constants, dark-matter couplings) are the way to frame the case as nature-testing, and she listed B053 as a case she would move toward only if the Higgs allocation could not be settled.
responses.response: That is the conditional I put to myself, and I now think it is met. My earlier worry was that a 1e-18 clock only measures something that is already known. The redshift-over-millimetres comparison and the constant-variation limits show that the instrument is itself a probe, and a null result at this precision is still a clue. I accept the answer on novelty, and I would add that the citation should say magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 level, which isolates the advance from the combs and the ion-clock prizes. I still hold that the clocks are less central than the Higgs, so I move because of the attribution problem and not because I have changed my view on significance.

responses.point: Pearce, the Chair, moved the clocks to the top, and observed that his own Higgs trio (Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra) differs from mine (Gianotti, Della Negra, Virdee), which shows how contested the allocation is, while asking that expert reports verify the Sr-lattice priority history before the names are fixed.
responses.response: His observation is fair and it is a large part of why I moved. If the Chair and the Secretary cannot agree which founder to omit, an outside reader will not be persuaded by either trio. I share his insistence on verification: before the vote the expert reports should say whether the early Sr-lattice work at SYRTE, PTB or NIST changes the pair, and I would regard a clear finding to that effect as binding on my vote. I do not agree that the clock avoids every problem, since the 2005 and 2012 overlap is real, but it is a question about novelty that the citation can answer, not about whom to name.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice-clock step (many-atom interrogation in a lattice free of first-order shifts) is distinct from the combs and ion-clock prizes, that the performance is already confirmed independently, and that the pending redefinition of the second should not delay the prize.
responses.response: I agree with him on the redefinition. A metrological decision by another body follows the evidence, and waiting for it would honour a roadmap step and not the discovery. On novelty, his tightly worded citation is the right defence, and I borrowed its emphasis on the lattice and the many-atom regime. I note his JILA lineage disclosure and do not regard it as disqualifying, since it is a connection to a laboratory and not to a credited person's work. I would still ask him to be as strict about the 2012 overlap as about the 2005 one, because Wineland's work was about control of single quantum systems, and the lattice answer is that many neutral atoms are interrogated at once.

responses.point: Mehlig argues for topological insulators with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the cleanest general mechanism, mature and confirmed across materials, and ranks the clocks fourth partly because the redefinition of the second is pending.
responses.response: I take the Z2 mechanism seriously and I agree with his reply to Eriksson that dropping Mele splits one theoretical idea. But my own assessment is that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission is a real flaw that his triple cannot repair, and his rebuttal of the 2016 overlap, while thoughtful, leaves some of us unconvinced. In the same spirit as my own move, I would suggest that a configuration that no one can fully defend on names is weaker than one with a clear pair. I do not think topological insulators are a worse discovery than the clocks, and I would be happy to see them considered again in a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports confirm Katori and Ye as the right and sufficient pair given the Sr-lattice priority history across Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE, PTB and NIST.
Whether the committee judges the lattice clock to be a distinct prize unit after the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or a late chapter in the same story.

Whether I am being too pessimistic about the Higgs attribution: the committee might accept a trio from ATLAS and CMS with a carefully worded citation, and in that case my original ordering could return.
Whether IceCube source associations will mature enough to be considered later, and how the credit among Halzen, Spiering, Karle and the AMANDA and Baikal precursors would be settled.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the lattice-clock candidates Katori and Ye, the Higgs candidates, or the other shortlisted names. My Princeton supervisor David Gross and my co-author Thomas Van Riet are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. As Secretary I commission outside expert reports and I have no tie to any of the experts that I know of. I have noted Kroll's JILA lineage tie and Pearce's astroparticle adjacency to IceCube and see no need to discount either.
